articles.title: The Open: Ryan Fox savours dramatic Royal Birkdale major win, admitting his hands 'were all over the place'
articles.summary: New Zealander Ryan Fox birdied the final hole in brilliant style to claim a one-shot victory in the 154th Open at Royal Birkdale; Fox holed a 12-foot putt to clinch his maiden major win but admitted his nerves almost got the better of him on the 18th green
articles.body:
The 39-year-old New Zealander produced a superb finish to the final round to overtake clubhouse leader Cameron Young and snatch a one-shot win.

Fox, who had carded a 62 on Saturday to put himself in contention to claim a maiden major success, looked to be slipping out of it after making his second bogey of the day at the 11th.

Back-to-back birdies at the 13th and 14th put him back in the hunt and he then did well to escape with only a bogey at the 15th after a nightmare lie in a greenside bunker.

He hit back by birdieing the 16th following a brilliant approach and then, after missing a chance at the 17th, nailed two superb shots down the 18th before boldly draining a 12-foot putt to claim the Claret Jug.

"To play that last hole how I did, I stood on the tee and said to my caddie Dean (Smith), we're going to try to win this," said Fox.

"I hit two perfect shots. I'm not sure how I hit the putt. My hands were all over the place. I was just trying to get it towards the hole somewhere. It's surreal that it went in.

"My focus with the putter all day was just take a really deep breath before I hit it and just try to hit a line, and I did that.

"I don't know how I managed to keep the putter face square enough for that to go on line, but I'll take it.

"Champion Golfer of the Year has got a pretty good ring to it. It is a dream come true.

"You do dream of this moment. I don't know whether I ever thought it was going to become a reality. Now it is, and to have my name etched in the history of the game is pretty awesome. I think it's pretty awesome for New Zealand as well. It's going to be big down there."

Fox, the first New Zealander to win The Open since Bob Charles in 1963, is the son of former All Blacks fly-half Grant Fox and the grandson of former New Zealand Test captain Merv Wallace.

"We've got a great history in our family," he said. "I was lucky enough to carve my own path there. I don't know if this tops their achievements, but it's certainly right up there.

"I spoke to my kids last night, and they said bring back a trophy. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them.

"I don't know if my dad would be able to contain himself when I was coming down the stretch. He's never been one who has been very good if he doesn't have control over things.

"I think when he was playing and in control of the output, under pressure he was fine. But when he doesn't have control, I think he's a nervous wreck. I'm sure he was."

Sky Sports Golf duo Dame Laura Davies and Andrew Coltart were both full of praise for Fox and the aggressive approach he adopted on the back nine.

Davies said: "He was the most impressive player all day. He stayed aggressive; I don't think he was scared of losing it. If he lost it because he hit a shot that just didn't work out he was prepared to stay aggressive and I firmly believe that's why he did it.

"He hit irons when he had to, but when there was a chance, a sniff of a birdie, the driver was out, full commitment.

"And the way he played 18 I don't think you could have drawn that up any better. Two of the best shots he will ever hit in his life just to hit that green to give himself a chance."

Coltart added: "I've never seen somebody push through the tape as hard as that right at the end of the tournament to win a major championship.

"At a place like this, too. It was just superb. The 62 on Saturday I think, helped cement his belief in his ability out there.

"While they all struggled with the pressure, he stood tall."

articles.summary: New resolution by the UK’s Green Party says the answer is YES
articles.body:

articles.title: LIV Golf: Competition secures potential $300m investment to emerge from restructuring
articles.summary: LIV Golf secures a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to emerge from restructuring before the 2027 season.
articles.body:
LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.

The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding , starting a court-supervised "restructuring process" that they hope to complete in early 2027.

It is unclear how much of the $300m LIV requires to start next year's schedule and which players will start the season.

The competition's participants are owed at least $45m (£33m) and have the option to leave.

However the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

League insiders see the committed investment as a "significant" step forward in the court-supervised restructuring process.

"Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season," said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement.

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

The credit firm, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams.

The financing remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions.

"This investment is an important step forward for LIV Golf," said LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil in a statement.

"We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.

Two-time major winner Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).

DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).

A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

articles.title: Lifeline for LIV Golf with potential $300m investment as league looks to continue into 2027
articles.summary: BC Partners Credit hopes to put LIV Golf on "sound financial footing" and take "renewed momentum" into next year; LIV CEO says: "This marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league";  Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau among players owed millions of pounds
articles.body:
Sky Sports News understands LIV has officially entered into an RSA - a Restricted Stock Award - with BC Partners and the league is confident it can move ahead with LIV 2.0.

The league lost its multi-billion-dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) following the end of the 2026 campaign and filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States.

LIV hopes a court-supervised "restructuring process" can be completed early next year.

This new agreement includes a commitment from BC Partners to provide funding, subject to court approval, with a hearing scheduled on October 14 to approve the deal.

The arrangement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until October 25.

BC Partners Credit keen to put LIV on 'sound financial footing'

Sky Sports News understands there is no obligation on players, who are owed millions of pounds, to stick with LIV, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts.

Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, said in a statement: "Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season."

BC Partners Credit will support the next stage of LIV, under which players would become equity owners of the league and its teams.

Major winners Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson are among the players who signed with LIV following its creation in 2021 having been lured over from the PGA Tour.

Those golfers are some of the creditors listed with unsecured claims - Rahm heads that with 7.5m (£5.5m).

England's Tyrrell Hatton (£2.5m) is among the creditors, as is five-time major winner Brooks Koepka (£1.25m), who quit LIV to re-join the PGA Tour earlier this year.

LIV CEO: We believe ‌deeply in the future of this league'

LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil said: "This investment is an important ‌step forward for LIV Golf, and I want to thank Ted Goldthorpe and the entire BC Partners team for their conviction in what we're building.

"We believe ‌deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players.

"We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."

The league said the funding would enable it to move from the planning stage to operational execution.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine Greens challenge Labour’s grip on Starmer’s former seat
articles.summary: Green Party leader Zack Polanski hopes to shake Labour, which has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – At a meeting organised by a Muslim group in London ahead of a closely watched by-election, candidates from the Green and Liberal Democrat parties made their cases to residents beside empty seats. Their Labour and Conservative peers did not turn up.

Labour candidate Sagal Abdi Wali, a Somali-Muslim woman, told The Guardian she did not attend because she had a prior obligation and the invite had come too late. But the organiser, the Camden Muslim Network, pushed back, saying that she was invited earlier.

Fifteen candidates are in the race for former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s old seat, including Green Party leader, Zack Polanski, who hopes to become a member of parliament.

Since the seat was created in Holborn and St Pancras in 1983, the Labour Party has held it. Starmer was first elected in 2015 and held it until his resignation, which triggered the by-election due to take place on Thursday.

At the meeting, the conversation ranged from local issues such as housing to Israel and Palestine.

Lib Dem candidate Patrick Stillman said his party had long called for Palestinian statehood but would not support a full boycott.

“I think the Labour government’s position is deeply cynical to apologise over Gaza, to recognise that mistakes have been made but to continue to sell arms to Israel, a country that’s committing a genocide,” he said to applause, adding that his party, which recently voted to describe Zionism as racism, supports a full boycott.

In leaflets sent to constituency residents, the Green Party focused on Abdi-Wali’s time as a Labour councillor and, more recently, as leader of Camden council – a role she secured in May.

One reads: “Bring change, Replace Labour, Vote Green”. On its reverse: “Every single Camden Labour councillor refused to sign the Palestine solidarity pledge or support pension fund divestment . Only Greens continue to stand firm on Palestine.”

Last month, Abdi-Wali spoke to the Camden New Journal, a local newspaper, about Gaza and the Green Party’s leaflets.

It was “obviously inaccurate” to say the Labour council did not feel strongly about the issue, she told the paper. “I want to focus on making sure that we’re able to put the message of what [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband is now doing with the government and on Palestine and Israel and Gaza and the West Bank.”

In January, Camden Friends of Palestine (CFOP), a local group that formed in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, presented a petition to the local council with 4,000 signatures calling for the council to divest its pension fund from companies involved in Israel’s actions in the occupied Palestinian territories.

Abdi-Wali, then a Labour councillor, did not support the motion. Rather than committing to divestment, most councillors voted to refer the question to the pension board for review.

“My impression of her and her politics is that she’s just really incredibly silent on everything, if there isn’t a career motive for her, and that’s kind of disappointing,” said 38-year-old Shadin, a resident and CFOP organiser, who plans to vote for Polanski.

“Watching a livestreamed genocide has made a lot of people that I know … disengage from mainstream politics or parliamentary politics”.

Like many London constituencies, a key issue is housing.

According to a “2026 state of the borough” report by Camden council, 8,380 households were on the waiting list for social housing at the end of March 2025, “an increase of 9.5 percent on the year before.”

On Friday, in the constituency’s more affluent area of Primrose Hill, one resident said they would vote for Labour in the upcoming election, while another believed that regardless of who wins, life will not change.

In Camden, another resident told Al Jazeera that while they live in the area, they were not aware of the election, as Labour canvassers buzzed to gain entry into a nearby estate in the background.

As both parties make their final efforts to secure victory, recent polls predict a close race.

In the 2024 general election, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein , a pro-Palestine independent candidate came second, with 19 percent. The British gambling firm Ladbrokes and Stats for Lefties, which examines polling, both predict Labour will win.

articles.title: Martínez-Almeida: “Madrid es una de las cinco grandes ciudades del deporte mundial”
articles.standfirst: El alcalde destaca el calendario deportivo de la capital durante la presentación del Open de España presented by Madrid
articles.summary: El alcalde destaca el calendario deportivo de la capital durante la presentación del Open de España presented by Madrid
articles.body: El Open de España presented by Madrid 2026 ya está en marcha y este año, pese a la ausencia de Jon Rahm, el torneo puede presumir de un plantel de enorme calidad que invita a no perderse una cita ya consolidada en el calendario deportivo de la capital de España. En la sede del torneo, el Club de Campo Villa de Madrid, ha tenido lugar un acto de presentación con la presencia del alcalde de Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida; el presidente de la RFEG, Juan Guerrero-Burgos; el promotor del torneo, Gerard Tsobanian; y los jugadores Marco Penge, Patrick Reed y Ángel Ayora. Todos ellos, flanqueados por la copa de campeón del Masters de Augusta y la Jarra de Clarete del British Open, y es que por segundo año el ganador del abierto nacional volverá a recibir como premio la clasificación directa para estos dos torneos. El regidor de la capital, que apareció en el Club de Campo montado en un autobús de la EMT decorado con imágenes del torneo, destacó el posicionamiento internacional tanto del torneo como de la ciudad. “Es un gran acontecimiento en el calendario deportivo de Madrid, como la Fórmula 1, el Mutua de tenis o la final de la Champions. El Open ya tiene personalidad propia y cada año entre todos hemos construido un torneo mejor. Madrid es una de las cinco grandes ciudades del deporte mundial junto con Nueva York, París, Los Ángeles y Londres”, declaró. De hecho, según el ranking que realiza la agencia Burson, esto es así y la sexta de esta clasificación es Barcelona. El listado de participantes este año cuenta con nombres como el citado Penge, vigente campeón, Tyrrell Hatton, Sergio García, Justin Rose, Shane Lowry, Nicolai Hojgaard, Patrick Reed, Francesco Molinari, Bubba Watson, Justin Reed, Ludvig Aberg, Thomas Detry, Alex Noren, Adrian Meronk… y una legión de españoles que vienen pisando muy fuerte como Eugenio López-Chacarra, David Puig, Ángel Ayora, Josele Ballester o Nacho y Manu Elvira. Tsobanian, el encargado dar forma al torneo, declaró: “Me comprometí hace años a que el torneo creciera y estamos cumpliendo. El dilema este año es a quién seguir en el campo. Año tras año hemos subido el nivel y nunca habíamos llegado a lo que tenemos en esta edición”. Asimismo, Juan Guerrero-Burgos puso en valor el crecimiento experimentado: “Esto no sería posible sin tantos apoyos. Por nombre de jugadores estamos ante el mejor Open de España. Se está tratando de buscar la excelencia y en ese sentido este torneo es una referencia. Hay que invitar a los aficionados a que vengan y no se pierdan este espectáculo”.

articles.title: LIV Golf encuentra su mecenas: un nuevo inversor aportará 300 millones
articles.standfirst: La compañía financiera BC Partners Credit quiere asegurar la permanencia del circuito
articles.summary: La compañía financiera BC Partners Credit quiere asegurar la permanencia del circuito
articles.body: La compañía financiera BC Partners Credit anunció que aportará una inversión de 300 millones de dólares (unos 265 millones de euros) para el nuevo proyecto LIV 2.0 de golf, la liga a la que Arabia Saudí decidió dejar de inyectar dinero el pasado agosto al concluir la temporada. BC Partners Credit informó en un comunicado de que este fondo busca facilitar el proceso de reestructuración de LIV sobre una base financiera ″sólida, sostenible y centrada en el trabajo en equipo″ con el fin de asegurar su futuro a partir de 2027. El anuncio de la entidad de crédito privado llega un mes después de que LIV comunicara la solicitud de bancarrota ante un tribunal de Nueva York y esbozara algunos de los ejes de su nuevo proyecto, en el que pretende que los jugadores pasan a ser copropietarios tanto del circuito como de los equipos que lo integran y que tengan voz en el diseño de la competición. ″Otorgar a los jugadores una participación real y activa en la liga y los equipos es una oportunidad única en el golf profesional y alinea a todos en torno al éxito a largo plazo del producto, tanto para el deporte como para los aficionados", sostiene el director de BC Partners Credit, Ted Goldthorpe. "Esta inversión es un paso importante para LIV Golf. Creemos firmemente en el futuro de esta liga y en la oportunidad de construir algo singular junto a nuestros jugadores. Estamos cumpliendo con nuestros objetivos principales, y aunque aún queda trabajo por hacer, este acuerdo marca un progreso significativo hacia una liga verdaderamente global, propiedad de los jugadores y centrada en los equipos, que complementa el golf en general y crea nuevas oportunidades para jugadores, aficionados, socios y la próxima generación de golfistas", afirma Scott O'Neil, director ejecutivo de LIV Golf. Para la empresa financiera, el formato por equipos de LIV, una de sus señas de identidad desde que nació en 2022, al igual que la ausencia de corte en los torneos, ofrece ″una experiencia única y valiosa que puede complementar y fortalecer el ecosistema del golf en general″. "Invitamos a quienes quieran ayudar a construir una liga de golf sólida y sostenible a unirse a nosotros", añade Goldthorpe. Este acuerdo incluye el compromiso de BC Partners de proporcionar financiación, sujeto a la aprobación judicial, y está prevista una audiencia para el 14 de octubre para aprobar el acuerdo. Además, garantiza una prórroga para que el LIV pueda negociar las condiciones con sus jugadores, y las conversaciones estarán abiertas hasta el 25 de octubre. Entre las principales estrellas que aún sigue ligados a LIV por sus contratos están el español Jon Rahm y el estadounidense Bryson DeChambeau, si bien aún no han confirmado si tienen intención de seguir o no ligados al nuevo proyecto. En el caso de Rahm, principal acreedor de LIV con 7,4 millones de dólares (unos 6,5 millones de euros), según la documentación presentada tras la solicitud de quiebra, afirmó el pasado día 15 que no será hasta final de temporada cuando aclare si participará o no en LIV 2.0 al asegurar que debe resolverse "un largo proceso legal antes de que muchas cosas puedan concretarse".

articles.title: Wyndham Clark Steps Back To Save His Career
articles.summary: Wyndham Clark credits therapy and stepping back from the grind for his survival as U.S. Open champ, proving mental health wins on Tour.
articles.body:
Life piles on fast for anyone chasing a dream. Deadlines, bills, and family events crowd the calendar alongside tee times. The constant buzz of bad news and urgent headlines never stops. Many golfers tell themselves to keep grinding until the wheels start to fall off. That is why the conversation is shifting toward taking a break for mental health.

It is not about going soft. It is about survival. You would not run a car for years without an oil change. Expecting to break 80 while using mud-caked clubs is something you would never do. The same logic applies to the human mind. Ignoring mental health does not make a player tougher. It just delays the crash.

According to MyGolfSpy , Wyndham Clark, the U.S. Open champ, opened up about the battles that nearly ended his career. The pressure was immense after losing his mom. He faced challenges that threatened to take him off Tour completely. Therapy and sports psychology are the reasons he is still competing at the highest level. He did not lose his edge by talking about what set him back. Instead, he found a way to use those struggles to his advantage.

MyGolfSpy reported that Clark is just one of several elite athletes who have embraced this path. Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian alive, publicly discussed his struggle with depression and the treatment he received. Kevin Love, a five-time NBA all-star, has integrated mental health permanently into his platform. These competitors show that facing mental challenges does not weaken a player. It strengthens their resolve.

The pressure for most golfers is not winning a major or Game 7. It is the everyday grind. Think about the last time nothing was clicking on the course. You worked longer, stayed up later, and skipped lunch. You told yourself to push through. That approach might fix things in the moment, but the real reset never comes during those frantic hours. MyGolfSpy notes that change comes from taking a step back. It requires space and time to breathe. Some golfers will play rounds, while others will hike, fish, or hang with their kids. Some will do nothing at all. That is the point. Every golfer deserves that time and attention.

The narrative around mental toughness in golf is finally changing. For decades, the sport demanded that players hide their struggles. Now, the data shows that addressing mental health preserves careers. Wyndham Clark's story proves that therapy is a tool for success, not a sign of weakness. When a player admits they are struggling, they gain a support system.

This system helps them handle the pressure of the PGA Tour. The game is hard enough without the added weight of silence. Golfers who take breaks return sharper. They are not broken; they are recharged. This approach allows players to enjoy the sport again. It keeps the passion alive when the results are not going their way. The best players know that mental fitness is just as important as physical fitness.

Golf fans should expect to see more open conversations from the tour. The days of suffering in silence are over. Players like Clark are leading the way by showing vulnerability. This transparency helps the next generation of golfers.

articles.title: Ryder Cup: Luke Donald warns against Team Europe complacency as Jim Furyk claims Team USA are underdogs at Adare Manor
articles.summary: Luke Donald is looking to claim a third consecutive Ryder Cup victory for Team Europe; American captain Jim Furyk says he will make changes to try and earn an away win in Ireland; watch the 2027 Ryder Cup exclusively live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Donald is aiming to become the first captain in history to lead a team to three consecutive Ryder Cup victories, having masterminded a 16.5-11.5 win over the Americans in the 2023 edition Rome and a historic 15-13 triumph at Bethpage Black last September.

Team Europe have won their last seven home Ryder Cups and are looking to extend that run in the centenary edition, live on Sky Sports , while Furyk has made changes to Team USA's qualification criteria and backroom analytics in a bid to end their winless away streak.

President Cup captain Brandt Snedeker said his victorious American team was "going to be a problem" in Ireland, despite needing a final-day singles comeback to avoid an embarrassing home defeat to the International Team, with Donald aware of the challenge his side will face.

"I have zero complacency about how strong the United States are going to be," Donald said in a press conference. "They always are. On paper, they tend to be stronger than us through the world rankings.

"Obviously we have a great record at home but again, zero complacency. I've seen what Jim [Furyk] has been doing behind the scenes, changing the stats, changing the qualification system. He is very, very motivated to come here and put up a good fight.

"I'm just as motivated to keep finding those edges for my team as well but you know and I know that the US will be very strong."

Furyk has been involved in every Ryder Cup in some capacity since 1997 and captained Team USA during their 2018 loss at Le Golf National, with the former US Open champion taking learnings from past contests into his second captaincy stint.

"We know what we're up against," Furyk insisted. "We also know that it's been 34 years since we won in Europe - there's no secret. I'm going to hear it over and over again, so I'm going to embrace it.

"Luke and Dodo [Edoardo Molinari] have the opportunity to set the golf course up, trying to tip the scales to Europe. We're the underdogs. I know it's always been played, we come in, the Americans seem to be the favourites.

"This year, there's no chance that that could happen. We're the underdogs. We understand that. We've got a lot of work ahead of us."

On who the favourites are, Donald responded: "For us, underdog is a mentality. We always want to prove something to ourselves, to the rest of the world.

"We understand that being at home is an advantage but we also know that the US are very strong."

Team USA have won just eight points from 34 in foursomes - where two players alternate shots with one ball - across their last four Ryder Cup and Presidents Cup matches, with just three from 16 against Europe.

Furyk is keen for all of his potential American players to be available for a fact-finding trip to Adare Manor next summer ahead of the Scottish Open and The Open, with the 56-year-old also looking at other ways to try and boost their hopes of a first away win since 1993.

"I'm going to ask this team to do more than any other United States team has in the past," Furyk insisted. "I changed a few things immediately upon taking the captaincy. You're always coming up with new, creative ways to create that team atmosphere and that bond, but we've got a lot to work on.

"I've had some ideas and thoughts about how I thought Team USA could and should be run in the future. I think Terry Clark, our (PGA of America) CEO, and I are aligned on those."

On the poor foursomes record, Furyk added: "It is not an anomaly. There's some issues - we understand that. Not something I'm very happy with. I plan on making some changes.

"As captains we need to do a better job - not only putting the folks into good pairings in good positions, but I don't think we are preparing for those matches in a proper way."

articles.title: Ryder Cup 2027: Captain Jim Furyk says USA will be 'underdogs' at Adare Manor
articles.summary: United States Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk says his team will be "underdogs" when they attempt to end more than 30 years of pain on European soil in next year's edition at Adare Manor.
articles.body:
United States captain Jim Furyk says his team will be "underdogs" when they attempt to end more than 30 years of pain on European soil in next year's Ryder Cup at Adare Manor.

The Americans have not claimed an away Ryder Cup victory since 1993, losing all seven contests in Europe since that victory at The Belfry.

Furyk, who oversaw a 17½-10½ loss to Europe in France in 2018, was handed a second stint as captain earlier this year following Keegan Bradley's team's defeat to Luke Donald's Europe at Bethpage Black in 2025.

"We know what we are up against, we also know it's been 34 years since we won in Europe. There is no secret, I'm going to hear it over and over again so I am going to embrace it," Furyk said during a news conference at Adare Manor in County Limerick.

"Luke and Dodo [Edoardo Molinari, vice-captain] have the opportunity to set the golf course up, tip the scales for Europe. We're the underdogs.

"I know it's always been the Americans who seem to be the favourites, this year there is no chance that could happen. We are the underdogs, we understand that and we have a lot of work ahead of us."

Speaking to BBC Sport NI, Donald said he was not entirely certain about Furyk's assertion that Europe will be favourites in Ireland.

"I think reading between the lines, he is very focused on this Ryder Cup and wants to make amends for what happened in 2018 and the last two Ryder Cups," said Donald.

"He's going to bring a very strong team, that's why I'm not quite so certain that they'll definitely be the underdogs. They'll be strong and will be coming for us but we'll be ready."

Donald, who won four Ryder Cups as a player, led Europe to a resounding 16½-11½ win in Rome in 2023 before masterminding last year's dramatic 15-13 triumph at Bethpage - Europe's first away win since 2012.

The 48-year-old Englishman made just one change to his team for last year's win but he admits there may be more of a "shift" for the centenary edition, having invited potential rookies Eugenio Chacarra, Angel Ayora, Alex Fiztpatrick and Kristoffer Reitan to a scouting trip at Adare Manor last month.

"Certainly something unique was that we had a lot of continuity with the last two teams but I expect that to shift a little bit for this one," added Donald, who is hoping to become the first captain to win three Ryder Cups in a row after victories in Rome and New York.

"There's always new talent coming up, it's about recognising that, getting to know new players, understanding how they tick and coming up with a great plan for success."

Furyk plans to change foursomes approach

In 2018, Jordan Spieth and Justin Thomas - two of the three youngest players on Furyk's team - starred as they won three out of four points as a foursomes and fourballs pairing.

With 21-year-old Jackson Koivun having impressed during an unbeaten Presidents Cup debut in last month's comeback victory over the Internationals in Chicago, Furyk says he is excited to inject more youth into the US side.

"I really love the guys who have played for us in the past few years," the 56-year-old, who played in nine consecutive Ryder Cups between 1997 and 2014, told the BBC.

"We have tough, gritty veterans who have been around the block, and I'm excited, we have a lot of great, young talent who have yet to play in this cup and I'd bet two or three of them will be at Adare."

During the news conference, Furyk said he will ask his team to "do more than any American team has in the past" to seal an elusive away win and vowed to address his side's dismal recent record in foursomes.

The US won just three points from a possible 16 in the alternate-shot format over the past two Ryder Cups.

"I know those numbers very well. I've lived them the last four," said Furyk.

"It's not an anomaly. There's some issues. We understand that. Not something I'm very happy with. I plan on making some changes.

"As captains we need to do a better job – not only putting the folks into good pairings in good positions, but I don't think we are preparing for those matches in a proper way."

The 2027 Ryder Cup - the second to be staged in Ireland after the K Club in 2006 - will take place on 17-19 September.

articles.title: Guernsey FC keep up winning run with Newhaven victory
articles.summary: Guernsey FC come from a goal down to win 3-1 at Newhaven in the Southern Combination Premier Division.
articles.body:
Guernsey FC came from a goal down to win 3-1 at Newhaven in the Southern Combination Premier Division.

Newhaven started well - Ezra Roag forced a smart save from Seb Shepherd in the second minute after the Green Lions had given the ball away before Lee Robinson headed the hosts ahead eight minutes later.

Guernsey's evening got worse when experienced defender Jamie Dodd came off with an 18th-minute rib injury before Jacob Fallaize was sin-binned for a remark to an official two minutes later.

But when they returned to their full complement of 11 men Guernsey improved as they turned the game around in an eight-minute spell.

First Sam Murray poked home George Goubert's cross from the left for his second goal in as many games after returning from injury.

Then teenager Goubert headed home an excellent 43rd-minute Dylan Graham cross from the right to put the islanders in front at the interval.

It was 3-1 moments after the break as as record goalscorer Ross Allen poked in Graham's cross from a quickly-taken corner.

Fin Du Port saw an effort curl just wide of the far post midway through the second half for Guernsey while Graham blazed an effort high and wide 12 minutes later.

The win was Guernsey's third in succession and keeps them seventh in the table.

articles.title: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court
articles.summary: Lubna Speitan offered to testify on behalf of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years after a Heathrow bomb plot investigation.
articles.body:
The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed after being accused of plotting a suicide bomb attack at Heathrow Airport.

Lubna Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

Court documents from 2015 show she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.

The BBC has contacted Speitan for comment. The Green Party said she holds no official positions and the party "takes all allegations of this nature seriously".

The motion proposed by Speitan, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy , called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Lib Dem MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Speitan argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

On Tuesday, it emerged she wrote a letter in 2016 to the New York judge in the Pham case describing him as "one of the kindest, honest, most sincere" people she had known.

The existence of the letter was first reported by the Jewish Chronicle and it has been seen by BBC News.

Pham, a Vietnamese-born British national who had lived in London, was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2011 after spending seven months in Yemen. He was found in possession of a live round of ammunition.

In 2015 he was extradited to the US and in 2016 sentenced to 40 years in prison after he admitted three counts based on his support for the group al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), an offshoot of al-Qaeda.

US prosecutors said Pham was directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him.

In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" of Pham who would provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state".

The documents said that would be "crucial in establishing a mental health defense", adding that "bears on the issue of guilt".

Speitan had a medical condition that prevented her from giving evidence in person, the documents add.

In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem".

She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed".

She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known."

There is no suggestion in the documents that Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other.

Speitan has not responded to the BBC's request for comment. The Telegraph reported that when it asked her if she remained friends with Pham, she replied: "Yes, it's still the case."

She was reported as saying she believed Pham had been "targeted" by "the system".

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate."

It came as Green leader Polanski grappled with division among the party's members , MPs and deputy leaders over the motion.

Some Green councillors have resigned since it was passed. Green deputy leader in Wales, Phil Davies, resigned and cancelled his membership on Tuesday, describing the motion as "the final nail in the coffin".

Polanski released a lengthy statement on Monday night to say he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

The party leader, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

articles.title: Puffin island Lundy on cusp of closure as it runs out of water
articles.summary: Lundy is in "real jeopardy" and could be evacuated if supplies run out, bosses say.
articles.body:
Famed for its puffins, the picture-perfect island of Lundy attracts birdwatchers from all over. But the island is on the cusp of being evacuated as water levels drop to the lowest levels ever, forcing residents to take drastic measures to ensure supplies do not run out.

Located in the Bristol Channel off the north Devon coast, the 5km (3.1 mile) long island is not the first place you expect to be running out of water.

It is rich with wildlife including puffins and seals and its rugged landscape makes for breathtaking views.

But speak to the handful of residents here and they will tell you of the battle waged since summer to ensure the taps do not run dry.

Entirely self-sufficient, the National Trust-owned island relies on a combination of rainwater and boreholes drilled into the granite for supplies.

Severe water shortages in Lundy are not new , with islanders and visitors previously resorting to bottled water.

But the hottest and driest summer on record has been a "steep learning curve" for islanders, said Lundy managing director Derek Green.

He said there had been no significant rainfall since April and it had barely seen 20% of the typical 1.5m (4.92ft) rain it expected by this time of year.

Reservoir levels dropped to 13% at their lowest, forcing emergency shipments of water from the mainland to the 28 people who live on the island.

Water restrictions are also in place for residents and visitors. Among the more extreme measures is the removal of plugs so tourists are not tempted to take a bath.

The island, which is managed by the Landmark Trust, is now pumping water from ponds used by wildlife to a treatment works as a "last resort".

"Bringing in pond water is something we've never had to do before," Green explained. "It's really our last chance saloon here.

"If we didn't do this, we would be facing the reality of closing Lundy... it would be devastating for us."

Green stressed pond levels had started to drop and a seasonal passenger ferry that has been shipping water to the island is due to end later this month.

"Hopefully the reserve in the pond will last until it rains but because it hasn't rained in so long, this is desperate measures," he said.

"We've got a working farm here and the animals need water every day... so to evacuate those animals, those people and to cancel all those holidays is something that has never happened in the history of Lundy before.

"It would be hugely significant... we're on the cusp of having to make that decision."

The use of pond water led to some recovery in reservoir levels, now at 23.7% full, but Green said islanders were simply "praying for rain".

BBC meteorologist David Braine said there was some rain in the forecast for Lundy, but it would take weeks to top up the groundwater and reservoirs the island relied on.

The very dry spring and summer followed record rainfall in the later part of the winter and it was only in March when most of reservoirs in the south-west of England were full .

Shipments of water on passenger ferry the MS Oldenberg from north Devon began in August.

The first delivery to the island of about 67,000 litres had been the biggest and cost about £7,000, said Green.

Since then, they have shipped 4,000 litres of water three times a week, with islanders using between 9,000 litres to 11,000 litres of water a day.

Getting the water from the port to residents has not been an easy process as the island only has a granite track and a handful of vehicles including three 4x4s, tractors, quadbikes and a fire engine.

Adding to the logistical pressure, a landslip in June closed off part of the track to the tiny village at the top of the island about 400ft above sea level.

Green said: "We have to offload the tanks off the ship and we have to bring them up to a staging post halfway up the hill.

"We then have to pump water with a fire hose past the vulnerable part of the road to another tank where it's then staged pumped to the reservoir at the top."

Island manager Matt Scantlebury said the shortages had been a "logistical nightmare".

He said the island's pub, The Tavern, had closed toilets and removed bath plugs to help conserve supplies.

"We can't have baths... all the plugs have been removed to resist temptation," said Scantlebury.

"People are showering with buckets to catch the water and then using that to flush the toilets and that's saving water.

"We've had to close the pub toilets so the visitors have all been funnelled to the back shed toilets because they aren't on our mains water supply... we now have to fill them from our pond water."

Green, who started working on Lundy in 2004, said water shortages had become more frequent and they also considered shutting the island in September 2025 when reservoir levels hit 33%.

He said the changing climate was more "pronounced on Lundy" and islanders needed to adapt.

"Forecasters are predicting it will be even warmer next year," he said.

"We've got to learn from this and be better prepared next year in terms of increasing the reservoir here.

"People need to learn to use a little less water over the winter... it's a sharp learning curve for us and the wider region."

Scantlebury said he was concerned for the future and it would hard to keep levels at a "reasonable level" without meaningful rain over autumn and winter.

"It's a trend we have to watch out for," he said.

Assistant warden Tara McEvoy-Wilding said 2026 had been eye-opening and the "brown, sad and crispy" vegetation was a visual reminder of how dry it had been.

"This year feels like the real first year people have been noticing climate change," she said.

"For Lundy, it's going to be a challenge going forward. We're going to have to be extra mindful and plan further in advance to maintain our water security."

As Green looks out over the "beautiful, remote and tranquil" landscape, he is fearing for the future.

When it next rains, it needs to pour, he said.

"I never ever thought we would have to take water from our ponds but this is the position we find ourselves in," he said.

"We're in real jeopardy right now unless it rains very, very soon."

articles.title: Ryder Cup: Jim Furyk urges Team USA veterans to "step up" to boost bid for historic away win over Europe at Adare Manor
articles.summary: Ryder Cup captains Luke Donald and Jim Furyk spoke to Sky Sports on the latest Sky Sports Golf podcast, recorded at Adare Manor in Ireland ahead of the 2027 contest; Donald chases a third consecutive Ryder Cup win for Team Europe over Team USA, captained by Furyk
articles.body:
Furyk captains the United States at Adare Manor next September, live on Sky Sports, having previously guided Team USA to defeat in the 2018 contest at Le Golf National before leading them to 2024 Presidents Cup victory over the Internationals in Montreal.

The former US Open champion has been involved in every American Ryder Cup team in some capacity since 1997, with Team USA heading to Ireland for the centenary edition looking to claim a first away victory over Team Europe in 34 years.

Furyk's tasks include trying to create a strong team unity within the American team and improving their abysmal foursomes record, having lost 26 of their last 34 matches in the format, although he has already identified other growth areas.

"If you saw our team room and you see they travel together, these guys get along well and they're fine, but we haven't got it done from a team perspective," Furyk told Sky Sports .

"I think we're going to go top to bottom (to improve things). We're going to start with the captains, getting them (the players) in better pairings and getting them more prepared in the way we practice and get ready.

"The way we look at it throughout the year, it's not like you throw these guys together 12 days out in advance and then you figure it out! This is a process and it's something we need to be thinking about all year long in 2027.

"I need my veterans to step up, take some of the younger players under their wing and play practice rounds with them. Let them know what the Ryder Cup is all about, what they can expect on that first tee and get them excited about making this team.

"That process is not a one-month window. For us it needs to be a 24-month window, if that makes sense. We should be thinking about the Ryder Cup all the time and it's something I'd like to put in place."

Furyk has served as a vice-captain for the last three Ryder Cups since losing 17.5-10.5 at Le Golf National in 2018, where he admitted his captain's picks left him without "horses for the course".

He said in a pre-Ryder Cup press conference on Tuesday he would "do more than any American team has in the past" to deny counterpart Luke Donald a historic three-peat, with Furyk prepared to draw from past experiences of being involved with Team USA.

"You would have to be arrogant to say 'no, we didn't win, but I do it exactly the same!'," Furyk added when asked about learnings from the 2018 loss. "Of course you wouldn't!

"I was getting started in that captaincy career back then. I'd played in a lot of events, but sitting on the other side as a captain is a totally different process and a totally different outlook on teams.

"I think I've grown as a leader. I think I've been a backboard for some of our captains along the way, with the experience I've had.

"To have that opportunity now to come back as captain for a Ryder Cup, and maybe pave the way for the future for this American team, is something I'm very proud to be asked to do. I take it very, very seriously."

Donald: I don't want an American win on my watch!

Furyk claimed in Tuesday's press conference his side were "underdogs" heading to next year's contest, despite likely having a stronger side based on the world rankings, while Donald is keen to lead Europe to more success in the biennial contest.

"I think we have a good process in place with a great team, people who work really hard behind the scenes, but every Ryder Cup is different," Donald told Sky Sports .

"It's a unique course, different players usually and you've got to bring something new, different aspects to make it fun and different aspects to get them in the right frame of mind.

"Those decisions are ongoing and really churning around the brain, but hopefully we'll be ready. I expect there to be a few changes this year. I think that's good, to have a little bit of freshness, bring on the next generation of players and get them involved.

"As I've said many times, I think home Ryder Cups still offer the most pressure to protect that record that we have - it's no small feat. Someone's American team are bound to win away at some point - I just don't want it to be on my watch!

"We've had a lot of success the last four years and we'll take that confidence into this one. We understand that we've defended home soil very well and I think that's something to lean into.

"The underdog is just a mentality thing for us - we want to prove we can beat the might of the United States. "

articles.title: Welsh Green Party deputy Phil Davies resigns over Zionism motion
articles.summary: Phil Davies told BBC Wales the motion would not improve the lives of the Palestinian people.
articles.body:
The Green Party's former deputy leader in Wales says he resigned over the motion to declare 'Zionism is racism' because it was "pointless" and some of the statements made were "disgraceful".

Phil Davies had been a Greens member for seven years, but had announced on social media on Tuesday his decision to quit the party had been "accelerated" by the motion over the weekend.

In the post he had described the motion as "imperialistic" and "idiotic", and that it "doesn't materially achieve anything in the real world".

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Davies said he "doesn't know why it was discussed as it doesn't do anything to materially improve people's lives in Palestine".

He said Welsh Greens leader Anthony Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to quit, and also said he hoped Welsh party members would vote to split from those in England at a conference next month.

The motion, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy , called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Welsh first minister says Green Party Zionist motion was ill-judged

Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court

Davies said it was "not the sort of politics" he wanted to be associated with, and that Green Party Wales leader Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to leave the party.

He said: "Our views are exactly the same to be honest with you.

"He sent me a very nice message yesterday as well. I class Anthony as a close friend and that will remain."

When asked on whether Slaughter would follow him in quitting the party, Davies said he did not agree with any elected official resigning and staying in the Senedd.

"You weren't voted in as an individual member under this system. You're voted in under your party banner," he added.

He suggested that Welsh members of the party should consider splitting from the Green Party of England and Wales (GPEW) to "stand on our own two feet as a Welsh party" in light of the motion.

Davies said he was "hoping they'll vote to leave" at their party conference next month.

In an Instagram post, Davies said he had not been treated with respect or been "given enough support from the GPEW".

He added: "I have often felt like the token Welshman moaning at various points, but have not seen enough action taken by GPEW.

"I also feel the position of Wales deputy leaders is ignored rather than supported by GPEW."

Anthony Slaughter, who revealed he had been diagnosed with cancer last month, said his former colleague had brought a "much needed new perspective to Welsh politics."

He said: "I am positive he will contribute a great deal to Welsh public life whatever his next steps are.

"While the recent motion is not the only reason for Phil's resignation, I know it has stirred emotions across our party as people express their positions on this issue."

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said on Tuesday that the Green Party policy was "ill-judged" , saying that he had always advocated the two-state solution.

He had been responding to Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner, who had accused "left-wing parties" of having a "sickening antisemitism problem".

Speaking in the Senedd on Tuesday, ap Iorwerth said he always advocated the two-state solution and stood "shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish communities in Wales".

articles.title: Open de Espana: Patrick Reed looking to extend lead over Rory McIlroy in Race to Dubai as he makes return from injury
articles.summary: Patrick Reed around 300 points clear of Rory McIlroy in Race to Dubai as he looks to become second American to be crowned European No 1; Reed hopes his success will encourage his countrymen to play more worldwide; watch Open de Espana live on Sky Sports from 1pm Thursday
articles.body:
Reed will tee it up at the Open de Espana from Thursday in his first appearance since withdrawing during the second round of the flagship BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth last month.

The 36-year-old - aiming to follow in the footsteps of compatriot Collin Morikawa, who won the Race to Dubai in 2021 - is around 300 points clear of McIlroy with five DP World Tour events remaining.

McIlroy is not playing in Spain this week but is set to appear at the DP World India Championship in New Delhi from October 15.

Reed has topped the standings since February after victories at the Hero Dubai Desert Classic and Qatar Masters sandwiched a play-off defeat at the Bahrain Championship, with the 2018 Masters champion also recording three further top-10 finishes.

The Texan said: "I've always prided myself as being that American that likes to play around the world. To have the opportunity to come over here, not only just play on this tour, but also to have a chance to win the Race to Dubai, it would mean a lot.

"[Gary Player once told me], 'if you want to be a worldwide player, you've got to go out and play outside of the PGA Tour'.

"Once I got the opportunity to come over and play, I really enjoyed it. Hopefully I can bring more Americans over and more of the top players come out and play around the world, help grow the game."

Reed 'uncomfortable' but 'able to perform'

Reed, runner-up to Shane Lowry at the Amgen Irish Open in September, said of the injury he sustained at Wentworth: "Never saw it coming. It was my first time withdrawing during a round of golf due to injury. I would rather shoot a million than withdraw.

"When I went in, the hand was all swollen. Any time it was touched, I was in a lot of pain, so they thought I might have broken something inside the hand. The hand was OK and it ended up being a shoulder issue. The good thing is it only set me back one week.

"It might be uncomfortable but at the same time I'm able to perform and do what I'm supposed to do in swinging the golf club.

"So no excuses - go out there, continue grinding and hopefully finish off the year strong."

Three-time Open de Espana champion Jon Rahm will not play in his home tournament with Spanish media saying the 31-year-old is in the USA awaiting the birth of his daughter.

England's Marco Penge is the defending champion in Madrid, while the field also includes Lowry, Justin Rose, Ludvig Åberg and Sergio Garcia, as well as Eugenio Chacarra, who sits third in the Race to Dubai standings behind Reed and McIlroy.

Reed, who quit LIV Golf earlier this year in order to pursue a return to the PGA Tour from 2027, has not played in the Ryder Cup since the 2018 edition in France, at which he criticised captain Jim Furyk's decisions as America tumbled to a heavy defeat to Europe.

Furyk is back as US skipper for the 2027 tournament in Ireland and asked at a year-to-go press conference on Tuesday whether Reed was in his plans, he said: "We are going to put the best 12 guys, the best team of 12. If Patrick Reed is one of those, that's great."

articles.title: Greens could face Brighton Centre ban over Zionism motion
articles.summary: Brighton & Hove City Council says the motion is not compatible with its inclusion commitments.
articles.body:
The Green Party of England and Wales could be barred from holding future conferences at the Brighton Centre after the party passed a motion declaring Zionism was racism .

The leader of Brighton & Hove City Council (BHCC), Labour's Bella Sankey, said she was "deeply concerned at the prospect of the Green Party returning to Brighton for future conferences".

She claimed the motion was "divisive, discriminatory and wrong" and was not compatible with Brighton & Hove's commitments to be a welcoming and inclusive city.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, said he would "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

BHCC owns and operates the Brighton Centre, which has hosted party political conferences for decades.

Sankey told the BBC she was considering refusing to allow the Greens to hire the venue for future events.

In a statement, she claimed the motion had "dangerously" conflated the right of Jewish self-determination with the actions of the Israeli government and risked "the safety of Jewish members and Jewish people more broadly".

Zionism is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland.

Sankey went on to accuse the Green Party's leadership of a "dereliction of duty", adding "the Brighton Centre is owned by all of us in the city and should never be a place where people feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs".

Green Party sources have rejected Sankey's characterisation of the motion.

Polanski, who is Jewish, said that antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state "are, and must always be, completely distinct - blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe".

He added: "It's our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK."

The Brighton Centre was used by both the Greens and Liberal Democrats to host their autumn conferences this year.

The venue has also hosted Labour's annual gathering in previous years.

In 2017, the council's then-leader, Warren Morgan, who also represented Labour, threatened to ban his own party from holding its conference at the venue over concerns that anti-semitic views had been aired.

articles.title: Sergio García: “¿El PGA Tour? Es una posibilidad... Vamos a ver qué pasa con LIV 2.0"
articles.standfirst: El golfista castellonense no descarta ninguna posibilidad todavía, pero tiene claro que quiere jugar en el DP World Tour. Intentará clasificarse para la Ryder, pero se pone a disposición de Donald para ser vicecapitán
articles.summary: El golfista castellonense no descarta ninguna posibilidad todavía, pero tiene claro que quiere jugar en el DP World Tour. Intentará clasificarse para la Ryder, pero se pone a disposición de Donald para ser vicecapitán
articles.body: Sergio García está en Madrid para disputar el Open de España. En el Club de Campo da algunas pistas de hacia dónde puede ir su futuro, pero no se moja del todo. Tiene el foco puesto en la próxima Ryder Cup Pregunta. Llega al Open de España tras lograr buenos resultados en sus últimos torneos. ¿Le motiva esto de cara a firmar un gran torneo? Respuesta. Sí, sin ninguna duda. En los últimos dos o tres meses he jugado a buen nivel y he estado cerquita en un par de en un par de torneos y siempre es bonito estar ahí peleando. De todas formas, cada semana es un mundo. Estoy con ganas siempre de jugar el Open de España y darlo todo en nuestro torneo y, si es posible, hacer algo bonito. P. Usted que ya tiene experiencia, ¿qué hace para tratar de mantener el buen nivel de las últimas semanas? R. Al final lo que intentas es estar mentalmente lo mejor posible, estar con la mayor confianza posible, disfrutar al máximo y luego ya depende un poquito de que te salgan las cosas según las venías preparando. Hay semanas en las que te encuentras muy bien y estás mucho más fluido, y hay otras en las que te cuesta un poquito más. Como siempre digo, si das todo lo que tienes, no te puedes exigir más más, ¿no? P. Ahora está el 141 del ranking, ¿siente que esto puede cambiar rápido? R. No sé si esto cambiará rápidamente o no, pero obviamente es algo que sí que me gustaría, al igual que seguir jugando bien y dándome opciones. Eso es lo que me movería en el ranking mundial. El caso es que si estás metida entre los 50 primeros del mundo se te abren muchísimas puertas. Hay que seguir peleando y veremos cómo evoluciona va la cosa. La pena es que sientes que a lo mejor durante estos años has jugado a mejor nivel de lo que de lo que dice tu ranking, pero sabíamos las consecuencias de los movimientos que hacíamos. Hay que seguir hacia adelante. P. De entrada aquí si gana tiene la opción de la clasificación directa para el British Open. R. Es un premio bonito, pero en cualquier caso no es no es la última opción que hay para clasificarse. Si fuera la última opción sí que sería algo más intenso. Pero hay que intentar darse la opción de ganar el Open de tu país, que además vendría con eses caramelito. P. ¿En qué circuito cree que va a estar jugando el año que viene? R. Vamos a ver qué pasa con LIV 2.0, pero sin ninguna duda estaré jugando en el DP World Tour. El más o menos ya se verá a medida que vaya pasando el invierno, pero es algo que yo siempre he dicho, que el DP World Tour siempre ha sido mi tour y siempre he querido apoyarlo al máximo. Obviamente, en estos últimos años ha sido más complicado por cómo se han se han dado las cosas, pero es algo que siempre he querido hacer y es el plan que tengo. P. ¿LIV Golf ha ayudado a internacionalizar el golf y a que los mejores golfistas se planteen salir más a torneos fuera de su entorno? R. Espero que sí. Yo creo que es algo que habrá que seguir viendo durante los próximos años. Creo que se ha comprobado el ambiente y las ganas con el que la gente nos ha recibido en muchísimos sitios en los que jugábamos. Antes había cinco jugadores buenísimos en ciertos torneos y ahora a lo mejor hay 30 jugadores buenísimos y desde luego eso ayuda. Cuando esos países tienen la posibilidad de tener a tantos jugadores buenos de nombre durante una semana, año tras año, la verdad es que se ve que la excitación es mucho mayor y están con ganas. P. ¿Cree que el golf demanda un quinto Major, que fuera incluso fuera de Estados Unidos? R. La verdad es que es complicado de responder porque los grandes son los que son desde hace muchísimos años. Meter un Major más que empieza de cero, pues la sensación siempre va a ser un poquito diferente porque no tiene la historia de los otros. Sería como el patito feo a pesar de que fuera un Major, sin ninguna duda. Esa es la sensación que tendría todo el mundo. Hasta los jugadores te lo dirían: ‘si tengo la posibilidad de ganar este o este, prefiero esos antes que el otro porque tienen más historia, simplemente’. Se trata de algo complicado. Son muchos años de historia y no es no es fácil de hacer. P. ¿Le ves futuro al golf por equipos que tú has vivido tanto en LIV? R. Sinceramente yo creo que sí que lo tiene. Hay que encontrar cómo, pero ya hemos visto que puede funcionar. Mira las ganas y la energía con la que han recibido a los equipos [en LIV] en muchos sitios. Obviamente el golf es un deporte muy clásico, de muchos años, de mucha historia y siempre que intentas salirte de esa línea, parece que todo se complica, pero hay sitio para todos. P. ¿LIV Golf 2.0 es una opción real para usted? R. Yo creo que todo es una opción. Lo bonito es contar con muchas opciones, pero la edición no está tomada. Cuando la tome lo sabréis. P. ¿Cree que se han puesto muchos palos en la rueda a LIV Golf? R. Es lo que decía antes. Cuando tú construyes o empiezas algo que es muy diferente a lo que lo que está acostumbrado el mundo del golf, es complicado. Mira, sin ir más lejos, en el fútbol, la Superliga. Siempre hay momentos en los que se pone difícil, siempre hay organizaciones a las que le interesa y a las que no, y cada uno tira hacia su lado. Al final, lo único que se te puede pedir es intentar mejorar todo. P. ¿Quién es el mejor deportista no golfista profesional con el que ha jugado un pro-am o ronda de prácticas? R. La verdad es que varios, yo creo que de los mejores deportistas no golfistas que juegan a golf sin ninguna duda, son los tenistas. Creo que son los que los que más arriba. Diría que el mejor probablemente es mi amigo Mardy Fish. Es muy buen jugador de golf, creo que es hándicap 3 o 4. A Rafa [Nadal] se le da muy bien; Juan Carlos Ferrero, que también es muy buen amigo mío, juega muy bien, tiene muy buen swing. Luego hay también futbolistas que juegan a muy alto nivel y también de fútbol americano. En Fórmula 1 tenemos a Carlos [Sainz] y Lando Norris, pero si tuviera que escoger, digo Mardy Fish. Rueda de prensa. ¿En qué punto está su contrato con LIV Golf? R. No está todo acabado, estamos en ello, el problema no es LIV 2.0. Pese a la situación en la que estamos de bancarrota, seguimos vinculados por contrato a LIV 1.0 y esto te impide buscar sponsors o acuerdos porque irían dirigidos a LIV 1.0 y queremos esa facilidad para buscar oportunidades. R. de P. Sigue habiendo incertidumbre y supones que no se sabe si habría repercusiones por parte del DPWT en caso de ser jugador de LIV 2.0. R. No sé realmente cómo acabará la cosa con el DP World Tour respecto a LIV 2.0, habrá que verlo. No significa que no vaya o que vaya a seguir en LIV, pero ahora cerrar lo de LIV 1.0 evita que haya repercusiones con ese contrato. Yo hago lo que creo que es lo mejor para mí y para mi familia y mi equipo. R. de P. En cualquier caso, ¿qué ha significado LIV para usted? R. El producto del LIV siempre me ha gustado mucho es algo bonito, hemos llevado un golf de alta calidad a muchos lugares del mundo que lo querían. Eso ha sido muy bonito y lo hemos disfrutado. Ha hecho que el PGA Tour mejorase respecto a los jugadores, todo eso ha sido positivo. Siempre habrá cosas que se pueden hacer mejor. R. de P. ¿Se plantea un regreso al PGA Tour? R. Es una posibilidad, cumplo 47 años en enero y es una posibilidad y también el Champions Tour [circuito sénior del PGA], que me apetece jugar algunos de esos torneos, sobre todo los Majors. Son cosas que a mi edad hay que mirar también. R. de P. ¿Cuál es su objetivo principal para 2027? R. Jugar a buen nivel. Es año Ryder así que quiero darme las mayores opciones de estar en ese equipo, que sería muy bonito. También jugar todos los grandes, si es posible los cuatro, y subir en el ranking mundial. R. de P. ¿Ha hablado con el capitán del equipo europeo Luke Donald? R. Sí, he hablado con Luke Donald, le he dicho que voy a hacer todo lo posible para estar en el equipo o que estoy dispuesto a ayudar en cualquier forma, como vicecapitán o como necesiten.

articles.title: UK Greens are wrong – Zionism is not racism
articles.summary: The party’s new policy reflects ignorance of Zionism and does nothing to advance Palestinian self-determination.
articles.body:
No notion has been so cynically exploited and distorted by both its supporters and its detractors as Zionism. Just when you think you have seen enough in politics to stop being genuinely surprised, let alone shocked, the Green Party of England and Wales has managed to do exactly that. The decision at its annual party conference on Sunday to vote, albeit by a small majority, in favour of a members’ motion declaring Zionism – which, at its broadest, asserts the Jewish people’s right to national self-determination in their historic homeland – to be racist, while supporting a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine”, was not only unexpected but deeply damaging: to the Palestinian cause, to the prospects for peace, and, to be completely honest, to the Green Party’s claim to be taken seriously as an emerging force in British politics.

Even before addressing the decision itself, one has to ask why, for a party whose raison d’être has always been saving the planet from the cataclysmic threat of climate change, the headlines at the end of its annual conference were about Israel-Palestine. They should have been about how best the UK could contain and reverse global warming, reach net zero, and address the many other issues that could unite the party rather than bitterly divide it. Such a focus might at least have given its MPs some spring in their step before returning to Westminster next week.

The decision itself to treat Zionism as “any other form of racism” is, in my view, a sad reflection of the sheer ignorance of those who supported it regarding the fundamental principles of Zionism, fuelled by hostility towards the state of Israel and, in some cases, intertwined with antisemitism.

The Zionist movement emerged in Europe as a reaction to rampant antisemitism, which in some places manifested itself through pogroms, displacement, persecution and systematic discrimination. It was also a reformist movement that rebelled against Jewish orthodoxy, seeking to change the course of Jewish history from within and enable Jews to become a nation like other nations, rather than remain a secluded and isolated minority living in the diaspora. Early Zionists regarded this condition as unnatural and ultimately disastrous, believing that it could be resolved not through emancipation alone but through self-emancipation – in other words, by establishing an independent Jewish state.

There is nothing inherently racist in the desire of a group of people who share a common identity, history, religion, traditions and language to achieve statehood. Judaism is not merely a religion; it is also a cultural identity and a sense of national and historical belonging. As the political scientist and historian Benedict Anderson famously argued, all nations are social constructs, or “imagined communities”. The Jewish people’s longing for self-determination was shaped by their biblical history of independence, followed by exile and persecution, as well as by the European ideology of a world composed of nation-states that took hold in the nineteenth century.

After much and bitter deliberation within the Zionist movement, it became apparent that the territory that appealed most to those who embraced the idea was the ancient Eretz Israel. This is not to exonerate the Zionist movement from internalising the deeply problematic notion, with strong colonial undertones, that the land of Israel was somehow a virgin territory. The slogan “a land without a people for a people without a land” encapsulated that profoundly mistaken perception.

The immense suffering of Palestinians as a result of the Zionist movement’s drive to establish a Jewish state in the land of their forefathers is indisputable: from the 1948 Nakba to the occupation of the West Bank and Gaza that began in 1967, to the expanding settlements in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, and to the horrors inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza in Israel’s response to the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023.

Yet the most fundamental document produced by Zionism – Israel’s Declaration of Independence of 14 May 1948 – envisaged a state that was both Jewish and democratic, without one principle taking precedence over the other, at a time when the Zionist leadership accepted the partition of Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Is there racism in Israel? Yes. It exists within Israeli society and has become particularly pronounced under the current government. Do Palestinian citizens of Israel enjoy complete equality before the law and freedom from discrimination? No. Israeli society falls short in this respect, and the refusal by many parties representing predominantly Jewish voters to sit in government with Arab parties, regardless of their political positions, is discriminatory and unacceptable in a democracy.

None of this, however, makes the state of Israel, or the entire Zionist project, inherently racist. The Zionist movement has always been diverse and has unfortunately included racist elements, but they have never represented the totality, or even necessarily the dominant tradition, of Zionism.

Practically speaking, the Green Party’s call for a single state called Palestine to be established in place of Israel is a shocking call for the elimination of an existing UN member state. UN General Assembly Resolution 181 of 1947 called for the partition of Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Israel was established the following year and admitted to the United Nations in 1949. What remains unrealised from that partition plan is the establishment of a Palestinian state, which requires ending the occupation and creating the conditions for genuine Palestinian self-determination. That is where international efforts should be focused.

Moreover, this intervention by the Green Party could hardly have come at a worse time: in the midst of a bitterly fought Israeli general election campaign. It plays directly into the hands of Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right partners, who thrive on the false narrative of “us against the world”. In this case, the Green Party has handed them precisely the ammunition they need.

The Green Party is entitled to its opinion on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, as is any other political party. There is much to criticise about the current Israeli government, the occupation of nearly six decades and the expansion of settlements, all of which obstruct the possibility of a two-state solution. But attempting to smear the entire Zionist movement as racist, denying the Jewish people’s right to self-determination, and calling for a one-state solution that does not enjoy the support of most Palestinians ultimately reflects more on the Green Party’s political immaturity, ignorance and moral bankruptcy than it does on Zionism.

articles.title: Suzann Pettersen: Two-time major winner to return at Aramco Korea Championship and could play 'five or six events a year'
articles.summary: Suzann Pettersen last played a professional tournament in 2022; watch Norwegian's comeback in South Korea live on Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports+ from 5.30am on Thursday, Pettersen "has nothing to prove to myself" as she considers further appearances
articles.body:
The Norwegian, 45, retired on the spot seven years ago after sinking the winning putt for Team Europe in the Solheim Cup at Gleneagles.

Pettersen played in the Aramco Team Series event in Jeddah in 2022 and will now tee it up again in Asia, with the two-time major winner having more time on her hands as her children get older.

She said: "Obviously, I've been playing and practising quite a bit at home. Nothing close to playing competitions. I'm curious just to see where my game is at.

"Coming here to Korea feels quite a long way to come to test your game, but I might as well just get the gloves off. I have nothing to prove to myself. I'm just doing this because I love the game."

Pettersen, who is eligible for the Legends of the LPGA and soon the women's senior major championships, added: "I'm not going to come back and play a full schedule ever. That's being very honest.

"I could ideally see myself playing five or six events a year.

"I want to keep the game going in my body, so I don't have to pick it up in another three years, and then it's going to be even harder.

"The clubs are the same. I have the same irons. I haven't changed much since last time I hit a professional golf shot, so we'll see how this goes."

"I think [the players] are all thinking 'what the heck are you doing?'"

Since stepping back as a player, Pettersen has presided over two Solheim Cup campaigns as captain - a trophy-retaining 14-14 draw in Spain in 2023 and then a 15½-12½ defeat in the States a year later.
